items.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: he fell in love with Chano Pozo and Patato Valdez, you know and Big Black, I mean these are great conga players.

ctx.x: Tell us about how that affects the sound and how that changes the style.

Well he loves rhythm. He loves rhythm, you know what I mean? He’s like the king of bebop you know what I’m saying? He’s like “titty boom, titty boom” so he fell in love with Chano Pozo and Patato Valdez, you know and Big Black, I mean these are great conga players. And he just loves that kind of music. And for me it was beautiful man because he taught me some rhythms — he taught me six-eight rhythms, and different Latin beats, but he loved six-eight rhythm, that are so simple, but still complicated you know? If…

You know jazz, what kind of separates jazz from other forms of music, like European classical music, is the vitality and the pervasive nature of rhythm. Could you elaborate on that and tell us how that rhythm is different in, particularly in the African-American community and in the way it enunciates jazz, than rhythm in other styles of music or other cultures.
